title: Practicality, Grit, and the New Face of Leadership
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Title Options: 

Building the African AI Future: It's About Mindset, Not Just Money 

Beyond Hype: The Pragmatic, Human-Centric Path to AI in Africa 

From Mining Shafts to Boardrooms: Africa's Blueprint for AI Leadership
content:
Over the past week on my podcast, The Angle, I’ve moved from boardrooms discussing sovereign AI to mining shafts where early leadership lessons were forged. The conversations with a bootstrapped AI founder, a seasoned venture capitalist, and a pioneering mining-engineer-turned-executive revealed a unifying thread. Africa's journey with artificial intelligence will not be won by the biggest budgets or the most advanced algorithms alone. It will be decided by a distinct mindset: one of radical practicality, resilience, and a fundamental shift in what we value in our leaders. 

The Discipline of Practicality Over Hype 
In a landscape saturated with AI hype, the most successful African implementers embrace a ruthless focus on utility. Ashley Anthony of Isazi.ai, a bootstrapped company scaling globally, frames it perfectly: "The words 'practical applications of AI' run deep with us... Let's build the missile for the bucket rather than building the extravagant vehicle." This ethos—born from necessity—forces a critical discipline: start with the customer's problem, not the technology. Too many organisations, as Anthony notes, make the chatbot their "version of AI," missing the opportunity to fundamentally multiply revenue or slash costs by 30%. For Africa, where resources are constrained, this practical, problem-first approach isn't just wise; it's essential for survival and ROI. 

 

The Gladiator's Grind and Investor Realism 
Scaling this practicality requires capital, but the investment landscape demands a specific kind of grit. Venture capitalist Kojo Annan describes the most successful African entrepreneurs as "gladiators." He emphasizes that beyond metrics, "there's a very strong human element... you have to have the endurance to keep going." Investors are slowly understanding the African story, but Annan highlights a key barrier: the entrepreneur's ability to clearly articulate the problem and the scalable opportunity in a language global capital understands. The success of diaspora-led startups underscores this; they often bridge the narrative gap. The lesson is twofold: investors must look beyond perceived risk to see the "leapfrog opportunity," and founders must hone the clarity of their story as sharply as their technology. 

The Leadership Pivot: From Technical Authority to Human Connection 
Ultimately, technology is implemented by people and for people. This is where the most profound shift must occur. Celiwe Ross, who led teams underground before guiding Old Mutual's AI strategy, argues that historical leadership based on technical knowledge is obsolete. "All of the things I've just described can all be automated. Can all be done by AI," she states. The new imperative is human-centric leadership. "The role of leadership is going to be to connect with people... to inspire, to motivate, to deeply connect, to empathise and sympathise, to coach." For Ross, this isn't soft skill, it's the irreducible human value in an automated age. This shift is crucial for managing the fear of obsolescence and building teams that can ethically and effectively wield AI tools. 

Conclusion 
The African AI ecosystem taking shape is not a poor imitation of Silicon Valley. It is something distinct: a fusion of gritty, problem-solving practicality, resilient "gladiator" entrepreneurship, and leadership that elevates human connection above technical authority. The call to action is clear. Founders must obsess over customer problems, not just cool tech. Investors must back resilience and clarity as much as innovation. And leaders at every level must courageously transition from being the source of knowledge to being the cultivators of human potential, creativity, and ethical discernment. Our future depends not on replicating another's blueprint, but on confidently building with our own.

title: Human-Centric AI: Balancing Innovation, Ethics, and Work in Africa
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Title Options: 

Beyond the Hype: How AI Can Empower, Not Replace, African Workers 

The Ethical Imperative: Building AI That Serves African Society 

AI and the Human Future: Why Africa Must Lead with Values
content:
In designing user experiences, a core principle is that technology should serve people, not the other way around. This principle is urgently needed in Africa's AI discourse, which is too often dominated by either hype or fear. Conversations on The Angle with experts from Vodacom, FNB, and academia moved beyond this binary. They revealed a crucial middle path: AI must be implemented with deliberate ethics and a focus on augmentation to drive inclusive growth and address, not exacerbate, our social challenges. 

Augmentation, Not Automation, as the Guiding Principle 
The loudest fear is that AI will cause mass job losses. However, a more nuanced view from Dr. Mark Nasila suggests a different focus: “We may reduce the number of individuals per unit of output, but we will still grow the number of individuals because we create so much more output.” The goal should be augmentation, using AI to make healthcare workers, farmers, and educators more productive and effective. This approach builds a bridge to the future of work, using technology to elevate human potential rather than replace it. 

Embedding Societal Values into AI Design 
Without ethical guardrails, AI systems will inevitably bake in the biases of their creators and data, perpetuating inequality. Atenkosi Ngubevana of Vodacom's AI Lab stressed this during our talk: “AI can be a great accelerator, but can further perpetuate the societal divide that we have.”  For AI to earn public trust and deliver lasting value, African organisations must proactively embed fairness, transparency, and social good into their design processes from the start. 

Smart Regulation to Enable Innovation and Protection 
South Africa's regulatory framework is playing catch-up with rapid technological change. The consensus among experts is not for restrictive regulation, but for smart, enabling governance. Nasila argued for policies that incentivize entrepreneurship and protect data sovereignty, while Ngubevana highlighted the need for clear "ethical AI" guidelines that are rooted in our societal norms. Effective regulation should create a safe platform for innovation, ensuring AI is used for public good while preventing harm and monopolistic practices. 

 
Critics may argue that an ethical, inclusive approach to AI will slow down innovation and competitiveness. However, the opposite is true. AI built without regard for local context and ethics is doomed to fail or cause backlash. Trust is the ultimate currency of the digital economy, and it is built on ethical foundations. 

Conclusion 
The future of AI in Africa must be intentionally human-centric. This requires leaders in business and government to champion AI that augments workers, reflects our societal values in its design, and operates within a regulatory environment that fosters both innovation and protection. By choosing this path, we can harness AI not as a disruptive force, but as a powerful tool for building a more inclusive, productive, and equitable society.

title: Building, Not Just Buying: The Case for African AI Sovereignty
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Title Options: 

Why Africa Must Build Its Own AI, Not Just Consume It 

From Consumers to Creators: Africa’s AI Imperative 

Sovereign AI: Protecting Our Digital Future in a Global Race
content:
Hosting The Angle podcast has given me a front-row seat to a critical debate: will Africa shape its AI future, or will it be shaped by it? With one in three global newborns set to be African by 2050, we are poised to be the world's largest consumer market. However, if we only consume AI built elsewhere, we risk becoming mere data providers selling our raw digital resources and buying back processed intelligence at a premium. The insights from my guests make a compelling case for a sovereign AI ecosystem built on our own terms. 

The Language Gap is an Innovation Goldmine
As a designer, I understand that solutions built for someone else rarely fit perfectly. Africa is home to over 2000 languages, yet the global AI ecosystem is overwhelmingly built for English. Researcher Vukosi Marivate highlighted this gap: “If you want to process social media posts in isiZulu, there are no tools. We don’t even have digital dictionaries.” This isn't just a technical oversight; it's a massive, untapped market. Building AI for African languages isn't a niche project, it's a foundational step towards inclusive technology and a major economic opportunity.

Underfunded R&D is a Strategic Vulnerability
South Africa invests a mere 0.6% of its GDP in research and development, far below the African Union's 1% target. Marivate pointed out the fragility of relying on external funding, noting how cuts to programs like PEPFAR impacted African medical research. The parallel for AI is stark. Dr. Mark Nasila of FNB warned of a "digital death" scenario, where over-reliance on foreign cloud and AI services could leave nations vulnerable. Strategic investment in local R&D is not an expense; it is an urgent investment in our digital sovereignty and economic security.

Our Constraints Breed Globally Relevant Innovation
African innovators are already solving problems that the global North is just beginning to notice. Marivate shared the example of Tanzanian researchers doing "machine learning at the edge" for farmers in 2017, long before it became a Silicon Valley buzzword. Our unique challenges, such as intermittent connectivity and resource constraints, force us to build efficient, robust, and scalable solutions. These innovations have global relevance, proving that Africa can be a net exporter of AI ingenuity, not just a consumer.

Skeptics cite a lack of infrastructure or talent as insurmountable barriers. Yet, we are a leading exporter of top-tier data scientists. The issue isn't a brain drain; it's a "brain lack", a lack of local platforms, opportunities, and committed investment to keep our best minds solving our most pressing problems.

Conclusion
The path forward requires a collective shift in mindset. Policymakers must prioritize and fund local R&D and data governance frameworks. Corporations must partner with and invest in local innovators. As citizens and professionals, we must champion and demand locally-built solutions. The goal is sovereign AI: controlling our data, solving our problems, and participating fully in the value chain of the digital age.

title: The Leadership Gap in Africa's AI Journey
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Title Options: 

Why Your AI Strategy Is Failing and How to Fix It 

Leadership, Not Technology, Is the Real AI Problem in Africa 

Escaping the “AI Pause”: A Strategic Blueprint for African Organisations
content:
In my conversations with leaders driving Africa's digital future, a consistent theme emerges: we are stuck in an "AI pause." This term, borrowed from the industrial revolution, describes the costly lag between a technology's arrival and its effective adoption. South Africans are among the world's heaviest internet users, and AI adoption is rising, yet most organisational initiatives fail to deliver material value. Our primary roadblock isn't a lack of advanced technology, it's a deficit in strategic leadership. 

The Peril of Starting with the Tool, Not the Goal 
As a consultant, I see a common and costly mistake: organisations begin by asking "What can this AI tool do?" rather than "What problem must we solve?" This leads to a collection of fascinating pilot projects that dazzle executives but die in isolation. Valter Adao of Kadena crystallised this during our discussion: “Less than 30% of organisations achieve a return on investment from modernisation initiatives... often the problem is that they started implementing a technology.” The lesson for African businesses is to first define the core objective, be it growth, productivity, or customer experience and only then reverse-engineer the role of AI. 

Constraints as the Engine of Innovation 
A counterintuitive insight from Adao is that innovation flourishes under constraints, not in a free-for-all of ideas. He explained, “If you add constraints to your ecosystem, then you become very deliberate in terms of what value looks like.” Without clear boundaries on value, timeline, and scope, innovation programs become chaotic and diffuse. For SMEs and large corporates alike, imposing these strategic constraints is a leadership responsibility that focuses energy and resources on high-impact opportunities rather than endless experimentation. 

Cultivating the Right People and Agency 
Technology transforms nothing without the right people. The focus must shift from finding technical geniuses to fostering resilient, agile mindsets. Adao emphasised, “The right people aren’t necessarily the technically strong individuals. There’s an attitude, a resilience... a mindset of ‘what needs to be true’ versus ‘why it can’t be done.’” Leaders must create environments where teams have the agency to solve problems, moving from seeking permission to taking ownership. This cultural shift is the bedrock upon which successful AI integration is built. 

 
Some argue that large, legacy-heavy corporations are doomed to be out-innovated by agile startups. While startups can move fast, large organisations possess scale, data, and resources that are formidable advantages if leveraged with strategic intent. The differentiator is not size, but the clarity of leadership. 

Conclusion 
Africa cannot afford a prolonged "AI pause." The call to action for leaders is unequivocal: move beyond the theatre of proof-of-concepts. Define your strategy before selecting your tech, use constraints to drive focused innovation, and build a culture of agency and accountability. By doing so, we can transform AI from a buzzword into a genuine engine for African growth and competitiveness.

title: From Engineering Student to Content Infrastructure Builder: Ndivho Manginya’s Long Game
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Episode 47 

On this episode of The Angle, we sit down with Ndivho Manginya — the founder of Panda Studios, creator of the Extreme Case broadcast-in-a-box, and the mind behind Media Plus, a local streaming platform. Ndivho is not a flashy tech founder. He is a quiet systems integrator who has spent years building the hardware, software, and workflows that allow other creators to look good.
content:
His journey from a small village called Chidimini to becoming one of South Africa’s unsung content infrastructure heroes is a masterclass in resilience, discipline, and the long game. 

"What I liked most was just to see the technical side of things and integrate stuff and make sure that we produce quality content. I remained in the background."

The Village, the Grandmother, and the Discipline of Chibasa 

Ndivho was raised by his late grandmother in a small village. "She made me who I am today — a resilient young boy who doesn’t give up." She didn't accept excuses, pushed for education, and instilled a work ethic that would later carry him through failure and reinvention. 

That discipline was reinforced at Chibasa Secondary School — a school that, according to Ndivho, has produced an unusual number of high-achievers (including Brendan Fernandez and others). When asked what they feed the students there, he laughs: "I think they feed us discipline. If you have discipline, that’s the recipe for success. You stand out from the crowd." 

After matric, Ndivho went on to study Mechanical Engineering at VUT (Vaal University of Technology). But first year didn't go according to plan. He failed one module, which blocked almost everything in second year. 

That failure, however, became an unexpected gift. 


The Switch: When Engineering Met Photography 

While repeating that module, Ndivho found himself with time — and a growing love for photography. His uncle had been the village photographer, so the seed was already there. But it was the #FeesMustFall movement that pushed him from casual photography into serious content creation. 

"I would be taking pictures of people protesting. I’d be part of the protest and also creating content." 

One video, in particular — a clip of Solomon that Ndivho shot during that time — is still doing well on YouTube years later. People call to license it for documentaries. That moment confirmed for him that content production was more than a hobby. It was a path. 

He eventually switched from Mechanical to Industrial Engineering (which included programming and mechatronics), but by then his heart was already in motion pictures. "There’s a saying at VUT’s School of Mechanical, Industrial & Aeronautical Engineering: it produces more photographers than engineers." 


Building Panda Studios: From Family Support to an NYDA Grant 

Panda Studios started as a photography and wedding film business. Over time, it grew into a full‑service video production and live broadcasting company. But the journey was not smooth. 

Ndivho is refreshingly honest about the support he received. His family — his mother, brother, and extended family — believed in him even when money was tight. "They would take from their salaries to support me. And I’m glad they didn’t push me to go into industry and use my degree." 

He also secured a NYDA grant of R50,000 after pitching at an event in Tshwane. That money bought a gaming PC with an i9 processor — still in use today, years later. "You can throw anything at it. It will still respond." 

But perhaps the most important asset was the community that formed around him. Friends, fellow creators, and organisations like the Thwane Foundation supported him with events and services. They shared a vision. And they saw that Ndivho was willing to sacrifice his last rand to make it happen. 

"It’s much easier for someone who’s just by your side to say: okay, if this person can sacrifice this much, then all I can do is support them." 


From Pain Points to Products: The Extreme Case and Media Plus 

As Panda Studios grew, Ndivho started hitting operational bottlenecks. He was using scattered software — OBS here, Blackmagic there, a separate audio tool, a separate graphics tool — all of which had to be integrated manually during live broadcasts. One mistake and the show could crash. 

So he did what engineers do: he built his own solution. 

Extreme Case is his answer to the problem. It is essentially an OB (outside broadcast) van in a box — a portable, integrated hardware unit that combines a video switcher, audio mixer, graphics computer, network router, power supply, and grounding devices into a single case (roughly 1m x 0.5m x 0.27m). One plug, a few HDMI cables, and you can control the whole thing from an iPad. 

"With this, you could stream side‑by‑side with SuperSport and still get the same results." 

A traditional OB truck costs millions. Extreme Case costs just over R300,000 (and Ndivho is already working on a smaller, smarter version three). 

Then there is Media Plus — a streaming platform Ndivho built during COVID to host live events, offer pay‑per‑view, and give creators an alternative to YouTube. The challenge, as he explains, is not the software — it’s the infrastructure. You need servers, data centres, buckets, bandwidth. You need to encode, decode, and distribute streams with low latency. 

"If I get a person willing to pay for the servers and infrastructure, the platform is already there. I could have Media Plus running again with just a few updates." 

But that infrastructure requires capital — and connectivity. And as Ndivho points out, South Africa is still battling policy wars over Starlink while the rest of the world moves ahead. 


The Ownership Question: Why We Need a Local YouTube 

The most powerful part of the conversation is Ndivho’s argument for content ownership. He is not against YouTube or TikTok. He uses them. But he is acutely aware of the power imbalance. 

"When you upload your videos, you think you own them now. But immediately you upload them, you’re giving the rights away to someone else. Someone may decide to turn them off. Remember the Microsoft outage? Companies were crying." 

He points to how China and the US regulate data: TikTok data generated in America is stored in American data centres. South Africa has no such requirement. As a result, local content — which is globally popular (South African dancers and amapiano trends dominate TikTok) — is shipped offshore, monetised offshore, and only a fraction of the value returns. 

"The content is money. When you create content, there are things you’re showing, things you’re advertising for big brands, things that are used to train AI. If you ship that content out, you are selling or taking away the IP." 

His proposal is simple: laws that require data generated in South Africa to be stored in South Africa. Then, track how much money that content makes for global platforms, and implement a fair‑use policy that pays local creators properly. 

"We don’t have to solve content consumption. We have to solve ownership. It’s done in Africa, it must be owned in Africa, it can be consumed anywhere — but the ownership remains here." 


Regulation vs. Infrastructure: Getting the Order Right 

Ndivho is critical of the recent parliamentary discussions about regulating podcasts. He argues that the government jumped the gun. 

"Should they not have started with creating infrastructure that allows creators to flourish? Instead of regulating, imagine you’re regulating me. I bought my own camera, my own equipment. You didn’t help me get it. And now you’re telling me what I can’t say?" 

He contrasts South Africa with Nigeria, where content creation is a national industry (a movie released every minute). "If we manage to create a community like that, then from there we can ask: how do we store it, distribute it, protect the filmmakers, the actors? But you start by getting the infrastructure right, not by trying to regulate before people have even built anything." 

For Ndivho, content creation is not just about viral videos. It is an entire value chain — cameras, software, servers, legal protection, distribution, monetisation — that can absorb thousands of young people into meaningful jobs. But that chain cannot be built if the first instinct is censorship. 

"If government is serious about job creation in this era of internet and content creation, there’s no better way than to create the infrastructure upon which content can be produced, owned, and thrive." 


What’s Next for Ndivho and Panda Studios? 

In the short term, Ndivho is focused on commercialising the Extreme Case (the broadcast‑in‑a‑box) and getting his live events graphics software into the hands of other production companies. He wants to simplify the workflow so that someone who has never used the software can operate it within 10 minutes. 

Longer term, he is still chasing the dream of a local YouTube — a Media Plus that can scale. But he knows he cannot do it alone. 

"Anyone with R10 million out there, please. We need a YouTube here. Send it this way." 

He ends with a quiet observation about the pace of change in South Africa: "We are still behind. Still battling policy. Still battling connectivity. But we are building." 


Final Take 

Ndivho Manginya is not a celebrity founder. He does not chase headlines. He builds things that work — hardware, software, workflows — and then he puts them in a box and ships them. His story is a reminder that infrastructure is invisible until it fails, and that the people who build it rarely get the credit. 

But without them, the creators have no stage. 

"We are more of a systems integration company than anything else. We must make sure that the system works first. Then we simplify the workflow. Then anyone can create."

title: From Township Streets to Tech Publishing: Philiso’s Journey to Amplify the Unheard
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Episode 46 

On this episode of The Angle, we sit down with Philiso Sebole — broadcaster, marketer, voiceover artist, and co-founder of Tech Publish. His journey from community radio and street interviews to launching a tech publication is anything but conventional. Philiso calls himself "the voice of the people," and his mission is simple: amplify the stories that mainstream media ignores, especially those coming from townships, grassroots startups, and builders who sleep on hard floors just to finish their code.
content:
"Who's covering the people that are here? Who's talking about their stories? You might find it's always hard to ask a non-technical techie to tell a story. They design things in the background. But you need somebody to tell the story."

The Gap in Tech Media 

Philiso’s observation is sharp: when you scroll through most tech platforms, you hear about Western billionaires or negative news from South Africa. Rarely do you read about the innovator in Soweto, the developer in a township innovation hub, or the startup that didn't raise millions but still solves a real problem. 

That gap became the foundation for Tech Publish — a publication that covers the everyday use of technology, software, and the people integrating AI, voice, and mobile solutions into local contexts. Philiso is less interested in categorising stories by vertical and more interested in the how: "If I categorise it in a certain specific that I’m only going to focus on this, I guess I’m missing out on so many stories." 


The Hard Floor Relaxer 

One of the most memorable moments in the conversation is Philiso’s story about a developer friend who sleeps on a hard concrete floor. When asked why, the friend replied: "If I sleep on the bed, I might find myself not even finishing this code." 

Philiso laughs, but the point lands: tech builders are among the most dedicated, sleep‑deprived, and under‑documented people in the economy. Their sacrifices rarely make headlines. Tech Publish wants to change that — not by glorifying hustle culture, but by showing the real human cost and creativity behind the code. 


Beyond the Funding Obsession 

A recurring theme in the episode is the startup obsession with funding. Philiso has spoken to countless founders who feel trapped in an endless cycle of incubators, pitch competitions, and grant applications — without ever reaching a sustainable product‑market fit. 

"If you just find yourself in continual rounds of funding, I think that's pretty much a sign your market is telling you your product is not worth it. The market has spoken." 

He is careful not to dismiss funding entirely — it can be a useful leg up — but he warns against treating investment as the goal rather than the fuel. His advice to founders: "At the end of the day, you're an entrepreneur. If it doesn't work, go for the next baby. Keep your eyes on the ground. What problems are people facing?" 

The title of co‑founder doesn't mean anything, Philiso adds. "The work that matters is the work on the ground." 


From Street Interviews to Corporate Partnerships 

Before Tech Publish, Philiso ran a project called The Phil's Drive — street interviews where he would walk up to anyone (from informal traders to famous entrepreneurs) and ask: "What are you doing?" That 10‑year journey gave him a unique lens: he understands the township market from the inside, and he also knows what formal corporates need when they want to reach that market. 

Tech Publish’s business model reflects this dual perspective: 

News articles behind a small paywall on their website. 

Insights from a research partner (no thumb‑sucking). 

Workshop coverage where Tech Publish handles all cameras, interviews, and profiling for corporate clients. 

Partnerships with telcos like Africa's Talking (they recently covered a week‑long hackathon). 

Crucially, Philiso wants to reach remote and township audiences too. By live‑streaming events and publishing street‑level stories, he hopes to bridge the information gap: "If I’m hosting this in Rosebank, you look at the distance, commuting and so forth. When we live stream such things or people read about it, it gives them at least a clue of where to go next." 


Regulation, Rights, and AI 

Philiso also touches on a less‑discussed topic: the legal side of tech creation. He recalls a conversation with a tech law firm about AI and voice cloning. When he lends his voice to an AI platform, what rights does he retain? What do cookie consents really mean? 

"Once you agree to the cookies, there are underlying things that happen. You're actually giving them access to that — which most creators don't know. To us it's like an easy buck, but from the creative side, another person might say, 'I created something much better, but licensing makes it difficult for you to use.'" 

Tech Publish wants to cover both the creator's perspective and the legal framework — helping founders understand what they sign away when they click "I agree." 


What's Next for Tech Publish? 

Kenya is their next stop. Philiso notes that while Silicon Valley gets all the attention, Kenya is a trailblazer in African tech, and South Africans rarely hear about it. Tech Publish aims to change that by telling cross‑border stories. 

In the short term, they are: 

Growing their website and social presence (@techpublished on all platforms). 

Partnering with research companies to add rigour to their reporting. 

Continuing to cover grassroots ecosystems, hackathons, and startup clinics. 

If you are a founder, an innovator, or someone who feels your story isn't being told, Philiso’s message is simple: "Pick up the phone, call me. We can figure it out. Tell it in your way." 


Final Take 

This episode is a reminder that media shapes who gets seen — and in South African tech, too many builders are still invisible. Philiso Sebole is not waiting for a big media house to fix that. He is building his own table, chair by chair, story by story. 

"I guess the moment that I don't ask you the question of what are you busy with, I would never know. So it's never about us. It's always about you."

title: She built an AI platform to put African creators on the global brand table
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Episode 44

"It's difficult to isolate it to say it's this one thing. It's everything together happening all at once. Financial issues, internal team conflicts, something breaks — that's the challenging thing about being a founder."
content:
That is how Boitumelo Olerato Moeca, founder of COVO, describes the weight of building a startup. No single crisis. Just everything, all at the same time. Sleepless nights. Bootstrapping. Fixing team dynamics while your personal life also demands attention. And yet, she keeps going.

That is how Boitumelo Olerato Moeca, founder of COVO, describes the weight of building a startup. No single crisis. Just everything, all at the same time. Sleepless nights. Bootstrapping. Fixing team dynamics while your personal life also demands attention. And yet, she keeps going.

On this episode of The Angle Podcast, Boitumelo unpacks what it really takes to build an AI-powered influencer campaign management platform designed to connect African content creators with global brand partnerships. She is a non-technical founder, a marketer by background, and a woman who refuses to let momentum die — even when the odds stack against her. 


From church socials to a tech startup 

Boitumelo's entry into the creator economy wasn't a sudden pivot. It grew out of her work as a marketer, volunteering at church, and running her own creative agency. "Content just surrounds every aspect of my life," she says. 

While managing an influencer campaign for a client, she saw the painful fragmentation: expensive manual processes, no centralised way to match brands with the right creators, and little data to guide decisions. That frustration became the seed for COVO — an AI-powered platform that vets African creators and helps brands maximise ROI using their own financial data. 


Creator vs influencer: what's the difference? 

Are all content creators influencers? Not exactly. Boitumelo draws a sharp line: 

An influencer carries the power to move an audience toward a decision — like a purchase. 

A content creator is anyone with a phone, a camera, and a story to tell. 

"It depends on who's asking," she laughs. For brands, influence is currency. But she insists that authenticity remains non-negotiable. Audiences can smell a forced partnership from a mile away. Professionalism, consistency, and creating a safe space online are what separate sustainable creator careers from one-off viral moments. 

"Authenticity helps people build trust with you — that's where the parasocial aspect comes in. But going further: professionalism, timeliness, and not being associated with scandals. Brands will look the other way if you're controversial." 


Niche depth, faceless accounts, and the algorithm trap 

How deep can a niche go? Boitumelo points to "looksmaxing" — a hyper-specific online community of young men optimising their appearance — as proof that even bizarre corners of the internet can become ecosystems. But in South Africa, where internet penetration is uneven, the creator landscape can feel more monotonous. 

Still, she sees opportunity. Faceless content — lifestyle tutorials without showing a face — and even AI-generated channels are making money, but they prey on psychological vulnerabilities. "People see a video and believe what it says without doing due diligence," she warns. For creators who want to build real influence, the path is harder: testing, refining, and refusing to chase algorithmic outrage. 


Inside COVO: matching creators, managing risk, and building community 

COVO is not just a matching engine. Brands build campaigns, set requirements, and get matched to vetted creators via a "Kov score" — a benchmark that analyses sentiment, past work, and audience alignment. The platform automates manual steps like briefs, content approvals, and payments. 

But Boitumelo is careful: automation can't replace human judgment when things go wrong. What if an influencer drops the ball? COVO builds in brand controls, web scraping for audience sentiment, and a strong educational layer: workshops on contract negotiation, red flags, and how to become a professional creator. 

"We're not just up for your money," she stresses. "We're building something with creators along the way." 

Her COVO Club events — Pilates days, wellness sessions, networking — show that community is the heart of the business. Sponsors like Bioderma have already partnered, turning what could be just another tech tool into a movement. 


Bootstrapping, vibe coding, and the Irish Tech Challenge 

As a non-technical founder, Boitumelo initially relied on a rule-based system and machine-learning interns from the Alix Ventures accelerator. Later, the team leaned into "vibe coding" — using AI tools that are intuitive enough for non-engineers to build functional platforms. 

"That was a tough decision because of the sunk cost fallacy," she admits. "We had invested money and time, but the new vibe-coding platforms had better turnaround time." 

The gamble paid off. Winning the Irish Tech Challenge — and a cash prize — eased financial pressure and connected her to European networks without relocating. 

"Try not to do it in isolation. Keep your relationships thriving — even if you can't build an internal team, keep your network popping. Those are the people who hold you up when you don't know how to make rent." 


Faith, family, and keeping momentum 

When asked what kept her head above water, Boitumelo doesn't hesitate: her Christian faith, prayer, and a support system that stepped in during her hardest months. 

"There were people speaking life into my life — 'we'll help you with rent, don't worry.'" 

She also cites a growth mindset: challenges are not blockers but puzzles to solve. "I might not know now, but at some point I'll figure it out." 

Her advice to her younger self? "Keep going. Even if you slow down, even if you fall, don't lose momentum." 


Data sovereignty and the African tech future 

Looking ten years ahead, Boitumelo is clear: Africa needs to own its data. She talks about data centres, telling African stories with African data, and building platforms that negotiate with Big Tech from a position of power. 

"It's a conversation around ownership, influence, and having a seat at the table." 

For COVO, that means being more than a middleman — it means empowering creators with education, safety nets, and a collective voice. 

 
 
Listen to the full episode above or watch the conversation on YouTube. The Angle Podcast explores how African founders, technologists, and creatives build resilient ventures in volatile environments.

title: Beyond the Checklist: Khothatso & Masentle on Building Local Solutions to Climate Risk
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Episode 34

On this episode of The Angle, we sat down with a formidable mother-daughter duo: Khothatso Nzimande-Manana, a seasoned risk professional turned tech entrepreneur, and her daughter Masentle, a Masters researcher in climate change and the co-founder of MN Risk Services.
content:
Their conversation moves beyond the abstract “greenwashing” debates to tackle a pressing question for South Africa: Who gets to measure our risk, and who gets to solve it?

From Spreadsheets to Startups 

Khothatso’s journey into sustainability wasn’t born out of activism, but out of a gap in the market. While working in corporate risk at Media24, the introduction of sustainability reporting (the "Triple P": Profit, People, Planet) landed on her desk. She started manually tracking data with Excel. 

What struck her wasn't the complexity of the work, but who was offering the solutions. 

"Most of them were coming from outside the borders of South Africa... there are no local players. We will forever be told what to do by other people." 

Frustrated by the lack of local ownership in the green economy, she registered a company in 2018 while still working a full-time job, eventually launching MN Risk Services—a firm focused on digitizing risk and ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) tracking. 

The "Interdisciplinary" Activist 

Masentle represents the new generation of climate thinkers. Currently pursuing a Masters in Interdisciplinary Global Change Studies, she explains that climate change isn't just about weather; it involves politics, energy, agriculture, and social justice. 

While she describes herself as an activist at heart, working with her "capitalist" mother has created a unique balance. 

"At first it was difficult... but as much as I want to be a climate activist, I still need to make a living. She reviews my work from a corporate side; I review hers from an academic standpoint." 

The Product: The ESG Tracker 
So, what does MN Risk Services actually do? They have built an ESG Tracker—an automated platform that moves companies away from manual spreadsheets. It quantifies carbon emissions from electricity, fuel, water, and waste. As Khothatso puts it: "You cannot reduce what you don’t measure." 

The Reality of South African Risk 

The conversation took a sharp turn into reality. Are we assessing climate risk correctly? 

Khothatso notes that South Africa used to "brag" about not being as impacted as the Caribbean or America—until the recent floods in KZN and hailstorms in Gauteng. 

"We are building resilience when the problem is already here... we are a bit reactive." 

Masentle adds a critical layer regarding policy. While South Africa has "good policies" on paper, the duo agrees that implementation is the weak link. Furthermore, regarding the Just Energy Transition, Masentle warns against blindly following the Global North: 

"There is never a perfect situation... We don't want to move too slowly and get left behind, but we also can't have outsiders telling us to go digital when it might increase our unemployment rate." 

Advice for the Hustling Entrepreneur 

For those listening who want to build, Khothatso’s advice is brutally honest: Sacrifice. She stopped buying luxuries, forgot to pay her own car creditors because she was focused on the business, and redefined what an "asset" is. 

Her secret weapon? Strategic partnerships without upfront cash. 

"We sold the idea to them: if we wait for money, we will never regain our economy. We have ourselves. We are educated. We met every Saturday." 

The Bottom Line 
This episode is a masterclass in why local context matters. While the world yells about net-zero, Khothatso and Masentle are quietly building the infrastructure for South Africa to measure its own path, create its own jobs, and own its own data.

title: The API Village: Africa Talking on Building a Marketplace for the Next Generation of Devs
author: Stanley Moloto
authorBio: UX/UI Designer, SME Consultant, and digital entrepreneur with a passion for building user-focused digital experiences and helping businesses grow. As Co-Founder of AddMore Digital, Founder of The Angle, and Director at The Digital Afrikan, I combine design thinking, strategic consulting, and digital innovation to create solutions that drive efficiency, engagement, and sustainable business success.
excerpt:
Episode 45 

On this episode of The Angle, we sat down with Graham Muhanga (Marketing & Partnership Lead) and Michael Kimathi (Developer Community Lead) of Africa Talking — a communication platform that has quietly integrated over 80 telcos across the continent.
content:
What started as an API business to simplify SMS, USSD, and voice integration has grown into a developer ecosystem of 250,000 active engineers, a marketplace 2.0, and a bold vision to run monthly hackathons in 23 cities. Their conversation reveals not just a product story, but a philosophy: Africa is a village, but it's made up of very inward-looking households. You have to localise everything.

The Accidental Pan-Africanist 

Africa Talking’s presence across 23 countries wasn’t the result of a grand master plan. As Graham puts it: "It was an accident — a beautiful one. The co‑founders raised money and just said, ‘Let’s do it. Let’s go.’" 

That accidental expansion quickly ran into real-world complexity. Each country has its own telecom regulator, different licensing rules, and unique banking challenges. Their solution? A core legal team that defines the workflow, plus local legal partners in each market who know where the holes are in the fence — and where the nasty dog lives. 

"You cannot do 40 KYCs, 40 securities, 40 banking relationships. It’s not sustainable. You are not in the business of opening accounts." 

The lesson for any startup trying to scale across Africa: play the long game. Sales cycles are long, currencies crash, regulations change overnight. But once a customer is onboarded, they often stay for a decade. 


What Does Africa Talking Actually Do? 

For the uninitiated, Africa Talking sits between businesses and telecom operators. Instead of a company negotiating with every telco individually (MTN, Vodacom, Safaricom, etc.) to send SMS, run USSD menus, or set up voice services, Africa Talking provides a single API layer. 

This matters because telcos don’t share traffic inventory. A business wanting to reach customers across networks would otherwise need to buy millions of messages upfront. Africa Talking aggregates that demand, buys in bulk, and resells to thousands of smaller customers — from startups to central banks. 

"Our biggest customer will always be a developer or a technical team that wants to automate their contact centre at scale." 

That technical focus is why the company describes itself as "engineering first." Most of their SDKs and API wrappers are open source, built by developers who needed them. One developer even built the most popular M-PESA API for Ruby — and keeps updating it. 


The Developer Community: 250k Strong 

Michael Kimathi (call him MK) leads the developer community. He points out that by the end of 2025, Africa will have over 1 million developers (Google research). Africa Talking’s goal is to reach 70% of them — and they’re already at 250,000 active devs. 

But they don't just count heads. The community is split into specialised groups: frontend, AI/ML, JVM languages, and soon a dedicated designer community. The logic is simple: a product needs more than code. It needs psychology, branding, legal, and sales. By bringing those disciplines together, hackathons become pipelines for real businesses. 

"We have seen people come to a community, meet other intelligent people, build something, raise $100,000, employ six people — and the rest is history." 

The Marketplace 2.0 is the next step. Developers can package their solutions (as Docker files) and list them for Africa Talking’s enterprise customers — hospitals, logistics firms, government departments. If a customer subscribes, the developer keeps 60-70% of the revenue. Africa Talking handles security, scalability, and customer acquisition. 


Hackathons as Education, Not Euphoria 

Most hackathons are frantic weekend sprints. Africa Talking does the opposite: their hackathon schedule is published up to 2029. 

"We give you a month or two to prepare. We are not about the euphoria of the moment. Let’s build solutions that last." 

Developers can see the theme, form teams, and build thoughtfully. The best solutions then move into the marketplace pipeline. Partnerships with Google (Gemini AI, cloud credits) add another layer: developers learn to build with AI while also using Africa Talking’s voice and messaging APIs. 

Prizes go up to $1,000, but the real reward is access to customers. Africa Talking now wants to run these monthly hackathons in all 23 cities where they operate — from Nairobi to Joburg to Lagos to Kinshasa. 


Localisation: Beyond Translation 

One of the most striking insights from the episode is how Africa Talking plans to localise its entire presence — not just language, but storytelling, testimonials, and even colours. 

"If you hit the Africa Talking website for South Africa, we will greet you in different local languages. You will see businesses that are running — the social proof will be South African businesses." 

To make this real, they are launching a Women in Tech Design Challenge: women in Uganda will design the Ugandan landing page; women in Nigeria will design the Nigerian version. A separate social media community will help developers tell their own stories, because traction without storytelling is nearly impossible for bootstrapped startups. 

"You don’t have a million dollars to spend on ads. But you can create lively storytelling." 


Data Sovereignty and the Cloud Question 

When asked about data sovereignty, Michael Kimathi gives a pointed answer. Africa Talking has already set up its own servers in multiple countries — not because it’s cheap (it isn’t), but because relying on a single cloud provider creates a single point of failure. 

"Basic engineering 101: you cannot have one source of failure. We saw what happened when Cloudflare went down — the ripple effect across the whole world." 

He also critiques the "open data" movement that promised to make government data available for innovation, but now often delivers three-year-old datasets. Without fresh, reliable data, local developers can’t build solutions that actually work. 

"The next oil was data. Then it became information. Soon it will be knowledge. And African history is mostly erased or misplaced. If we lose that, everything becomes slower." 

His bottom line: African governments need to mandate local data hosting (at least 50%), and pan-African banks need to offer single KYC across borders. Otherwise, the continent will keep exporting its data and importing expensive solutions. 


What Startups Can Expect from Africa Talking 

If you’re a startup or a solo developer, here’s what Africa Talking offers right now: 

Sandbox environment – free credits to test APIs in a live setting (up to two weeks). 

Access to engineers – if you spend $1,000 on their platform but lack in‑house devs, they will project‑manage a solution for you using their network of engineers. 

Marketplace listing – package your solution once, and let enterprise customers find you. 

Networking events – they are relaunching collision spaces where startups meet Africa Talking’s existing customers (governments, logistics firms, hospitals). 

"Some of the startups today are building incredible things that our customers really need. We can orchestrate that collision." 


The Long View 

The episode closes with a sobering reflection on Africa’s development timeline. The African Union’s Agenda 2063 envisions the continent they want — but that’s nearly 40 years from now. 

Graham’s response is part frustration, part resolve: 

"Governments and presidents are diligently working on this agenda… that they will leave for the next one to carry. That’s crazy. The turnaround time for a lot of things in Africa is in the woods." 

Yet Africa Talking keeps building — one API, one hackathon, one localised landing page at a time. Their message to developers across the continent is simple: You don’t need to leave. The infrastructure is here. The community is here. Now build.
